titolo: Barings – How One Trader Broke the Queen's Bank
descrizione:
In February 1995, Barings, Britain's oldest merchant bank, founded in 1762, collapsed after losses of about £827 million on futures and options positions in Singapore. This documentary retraces how a single trader, Nick Leeson, hid his losses in an error account numbered 88888, and how weak internal controls let the problem grow unseen.

We follow the timeline from his arrival in Singapore, through the Kobe earthquake of 17 January 1995, to the bank's sale to ING for £1 on 6 March 1995. Sources include the Bank of England's Board of Banking Supervision report of July 1995 and the reporting of major newspapers.

copertina.scena_rosso: A lone trader in a red suit stands at a trading desk, frantically stacking glowing contracts higher and higher while hiding a ledger behind his back
copertina.scena_blu: A group of blue-suited bankers in a distant London boardroom look the other way at charts and reports, unaware of the danger behind them
copertina.scena_oro: A gold crest of an old bank cracks down the middle and begins to crumble into falling coins

fatti: Barings Bank was founded in 1762 and was Britain's oldest merchant bank
It collapsed in late February 1995, with losses of about £827 million
The losses exceeded the bank's total capital, per the Bank of England report
The losses came from a single trader in Singapore
Open question: how could one young trader hide a hole that size from an entire bank? (answered at the end)
Barings was founded in London in 1762
It had financed governments and major historical events, including the Louisiana Purchase of 1803
It was a famous name in British finance
By the 1990s the securities business was a growing part of the group, including operations in Asia
Nick Leeson was born in 1967 and joined Barings in 1992
He was sent to Singapore, where Barings Futures (Singapore) traded on SIMEX, the Singapore International Monetary Exchange
He was both head of trading and head of settlement operations, a combination that removed the normal separation of duties
The Bank of England report identified this lack of segregation as a key failure
Error account number 88888 was opened in July 1992
Such accounts normally record small trading mistakes
Leeson used it to hide losing trades from London
Barings headquarters did not detect the growing losses held there
The hidden losses increased through 1993 and 1994
Leeson traded Nikkei 225 futures and options on SIMEX and Osaka
He had been authorised for arbitrage, small price differences between markets, which is low-risk
Instead he took large directional bets on the direction of the Nikkei, per the Bank of England report
When bets lost, he increased positions hoping to recover, a pattern of doubling down
Barings sent large sums to fund his margin calls, in part because London misunderstood the nature of the business
Leeson held a large short straddle position betting the Nikkei would stay stable
The Kobe earthquake struck on 17 January 1995
The Nikkei 225 fell sharply afterwards
He responded by buying huge numbers of Nikkei futures contracts, betting on a rebound
The market continued to fall and his losses grew
Losses grew to hundreds of millions of pounds in a few weeks
Barings had sent hundreds of millions of pounds to Singapore to cover margin calls, per the Bank of England report
Auditors and internal staff had raised concerns earlier, but they were not acted on decisively
Leeson left Singapore on 23 February 1995, leaving a note saying he was sorry
Barings discovered the full scale of the problem after his departure
The Bank of England tried to arrange a rescue over the weekend of 25–26 February 1995 but failed
Barings was placed into administration on 26 February 1995
Dutch financial group ING bought Barings on 6 March 1995 for a symbolic £1 and took on its liabilities
Final losses were reported at about £827 million
Leeson was arrested in Frankfurt on 2 March 1995 and was sentenced in Singapore in December 1995 to six and a half years in prison; he was released in 1999
The Board of Banking Supervision published its report in July 1995
It found senior management failed to understand the business and did not enforce controls
Leeson's dual role as trader and back-office head was never separated
London treated profits reported from Singapore as proof of success without checking the risk behind them
Answer to the opening loop: no single control stopped him, because the bank had removed the checks that should have
Separation of trading and settlement became a basic rule of risk control across banking
Barings became a standard case study in operational risk
Later rogue trader cases, such as Société Générale in 2008, showed similar control failures
Unusually high profits from low-risk strategies should trigger questions, not applause
End with: Subscribe for the next one.

_correzioni: Description: 'collapsed after losses of about £827 million' kept (well documented); Kobe earthquake date 17 January 1995 and sale to ING 6 March 1995 for £1 confirmed

Chapter 1: 'roughly twice the bank's available capital' corrected to 'exceeded the bank's total capital' (losses were about 2x its capital is widely cited, but the BoE report wording is that they exceeded capital; made safer)
Chapter 1: 'one 28-year-old' kept (Leeson was 28 in Feb 1995, born 25 Feb 1967 so he turned 28 on 25 Feb 1995; changed to 'a young trader' for safety)
Chapter 2: Louisiana Purchase of 1803 kept (Barings and Hope & Co financed it); 'Royal family' clients claim removed as unverified
Chapter 3: Leeson joined Barings in 1992 and went to Singapore in 1992 - confirmed; 'head of settlement operations' kept (documented)
Chapter 4: error account 88888 opened in July 1992 confirmed (reported opened 1992); 'increased through 1993 and 1994' kept
Chapter 5: 'Barings sent large sums to fund margin calls, in part because London misunderstood the business' kept; BoE finding on unauthorised directional trades kept
Chapter 6: 'short straddle' on Nikkei kept, confirmed by BoE report

Chapter 7: £742 million sent to Singapore is not reliably documented; replaced with 'more than £700 million' wording avoided and changed to 'hundreds of millions of pounds', as the commonly cited figure is about £742m but sources vary; removed specific figure
Chapter 7: Leeson left Singapore on 23 February 1995 confirmed; note saying 'I'm sorry' confirmed
Chapter 8: Barings placed in administration on 26 February 1995 confirmed; rescue attempt over weekend 25-26 Feb confirmed
Chapter 8: Leeson arrested in Frankfurt on 2 March 1995 confirmed; sentenced 2 December 1995 to six and a half years confirmed; released in 1999 (July 1999) confirmed
Chapter 9: BoE Board of Banking Supervision report published July 1995 confirmed
Tag 'Billion Ruin' removed as unverifiable/non-standard term
